contact_edits.before: The play juxtaposes, and exposes, two barren marriages. While George and Martha delight in stripping their marital scars in company, Nick and Honey have theirs dragged, cajoled or threatened out of them -- and they're at least equally grievous. As Nick, envied and mocked by George as the wave of the scientific future, Tim Campbell is perfect: broad-shouldered, self-satisfied, his limited sympathies subsiding as his insecurities increase. The recurring description of Diana Donnelly's Honey as "slim-hipped" here seems like just another of the characters' games but she beautifully registers the trophy bride's progress from delicious shock to shock absolute. Fine as all four performances are individually, the real prize of Diana Leblanc's production is the phenomenal degree of contact between them. There is never a moment at which either action or reaction goes slack, and both the pacing and the placing are impeccable. Astrid Janson's gaunt, precipitous set is a suitably gladiatorial arena, with a couple of oddities. The books are mostly painted, suggesting that even the household's literacy is suspect, and the shelves are adorned with pictures of George and Martha's namesakes, the Washingtons: Is this the production getting cute or are the characters? I still have doubts as to whether the play signifies much beyond its very enjoyable self. But that self is substantial: dialogue that stings, action that builds, characters who've become archetypes and -- it now appears -- compassion. In its 11 years, Soulpepper has given us any number of good productions and a handful of great ones. This is one of the greats. - Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf ? is in repertory through Oct. 24 at the Young Centre. For tickets and information visit soulpepper.caor call 416-866-8666. robert.cushman@hotmail.com
